title: Deficiency and Malabsorption Conditions
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter explains why nutrients fail to reach the blood when the stomach stops making acid, when the small intestinal mucosa is damaged, when digestive enzymes are missing, when bowel is removed, and when bacteria colonize a stagnant loop. Each condition is a break at a predictable step: luminal digestion, brush border digestion, mucosal uptake, or ileal recycling of bile acids and vitamin B12. Board questions give the stool, the anemia, the vitamin pattern, and one or two tests (D-xylose, fecal elastase, breath hydrogen, gastrin, folate) and ask you to name the step that failed. If you can place a disorder on that sequence, its findings follow.
prerequisites: Gastric parietal, chief, G, D, and ECL cells and the control of acid secretion
Luminal and brush border digestion of carbohydrate, protein, and fat (GI-6)
Micelle formation, enterohepatic circulation of bile acids, and sites of nutrient absorption (GI-7)
Iron, folate, and vitamin B12 metabolism and the megaloblastic anemias
MHC class II antigen presentation and CD4 and CD8 T cell effector functions

connections.how: Celiac disease and autoimmune gastritis are T cell driven diseases whose antibodies serve as diagnostic markers rather than the main cause of injury.
Loss of pancreatic enzyme output is the main luminal cause of steatorrhea and is separated from mucosal disease by fecal elastase and D-xylose.
The type of anemia (microcytic from iron, macrocytic from B12 or folate) points to the segment of bowel or the gastric function that has failed.
Fat malabsorption with an intact colon raises oxalate absorption and produces calcium oxalate kidney stones.
Hypergastrinemia drives ECL cell carcinoid tumors, and chronic celiac inflammation raises the risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.

terms.def: Absence of hydrochloric acid secretion by the stomach, usually from loss of parietal cells.
A raised serum gastrin level, appropriate when gastric acid is absent and inappropriate when it comes from a gastrinoma.
A histamine-secreting neuroendocrine cell of the gastric body and fundus whose growth is stimulated by gastrin.
Defective digestion, mucosal uptake, or transport of nutrients, with loss of those nutrients in the stool.
Excess fat in the stool, classically more than about 7 g per day on a diet containing about 100 g of fat.
Shortening and flattening of small intestinal villi that reduces absorptive surface area.
A T lymphocyte, mostly CD8 positive, that sits between enterocytes above the basement membrane.
Measurement of blood or urine xylose after an oral dose of this pentose, which is absorbed without digestion and so tests mucosal uptake.
A pancreatic protease that survives intestinal transit; a low stool level indicates reduced pancreatic exocrine output.
A duodenal brush border protease, also called enterokinase, that converts trypsinogen to trypsin.
Measured stool osmolality (taken as about 290 mOsm/kg) minus twice the sum of stool Na+ and K+; a large gap means unabsorbed solute is holding water.
Increased colonic absorption and urinary excretion of oxalate caused by fat malabsorption.

blocks.text: Parietal cells in the oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body and fundus secrete H+ through the H+/K+ ATPase and also secrete intrinsic factor. Gastrin from antral G cells stimulates acid secretion, mostly indirectly by making ECL cells release histamine. Acid limits its own stimulus: when antral pH falls below about 3, D cells release somatostatin, which suppresses gastrin. Achlorhydria therefore removes a brake as well as an acid.

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is the classic cause. CD4 T cells directed against the H+/K+ ATPase destroy parietal cells in the body and fundus, while the antrum, which has no parietal cells, is spared. Antibodies to parietal cells and to intrinsic factor are markers of the process. Chief cells are lost along with parietal cells, so serum pepsinogen I falls. Chronic H. pylori infection that spreads from the antrum into the body (pangastritis) causes multifocal atrophy with intestinal metaplasia and hypochlorhydria. Because the antrum is also inflamed, gastrin rises less than in autoimmune disease. Gastrectomy removes parietal cells directly; a distal resection also removes the antrum and its G cells, so gastrin does not rise.

blocks.title: Autoimmune gastritis to gastric carcinoid
steps: T cells destroy parietal cells in body and fundus
Acid secretion fails; antral pH stays high
D cells release little somatostatin
Antral G cells secrete gastrin without restraint
Gastrin stimulates ECL cell hyperplasia
ECL hyperplasia can progress to type 1 gastric carcinoid
blocks.caption: The antrum is spared, so the loss of acid feedback produces sustained hypergastrinemia, which is trophic to ECL cells.

blocks.text: Gastrin is a growth factor for ECL cells. Sustained hypergastrinemia produces linear and then nodular ECL cell hyperplasia, which can progress to type 1 gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors, usually small and multiple. Atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia also raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. A high gastrin level means something different depending on gastric pH: with achlorhydria it is an appropriate response to absent acid, while with very low pH it suggests autonomous secretion by a gastrinoma.

The nutrient consequences follow from what acid does. Dietary nonheme iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+), which precipitates at neutral pH. Acid keeps it soluble and favors its reduction to ferrous iron (Fe2+) by duodenal cytochrome b, the form carried by DMT1, so achlorhydria causes iron deficiency. Acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from food proteins so it can bind haptocorrin and later intrinsic factor. Achlorhydria alone causes food-bound B12 malabsorption; autoimmune gastritis adds loss of intrinsic factor, producing pernicious anemia. Acid also kills swallowed organisms, so its loss permits bacterial overgrowth in the stomach and proximal small bowel and increases susceptibility to enteric infection.

blocks.title: Consequences of achlorhydria
rows: No acid-driven somatostatin brake on antral G cells
Gastrin is trophic to ECL cells
Chief cells lost with oxyntic mucosa
B12 not freed from food; intrinsic factor lost in autoimmune disease
Loss of the gastric acid barrier
blocks.caption: Distal gastrectomy removes the antrum, so it causes the nutrient findings without hypergastrinemia.

blocks.predict: Two patients have fasting gastrin levels many times normal. One has a gastric pH of 7, the other a pH of 1.5 with multiple duodenal ulcers. Which patient has ECL hyperplasia as a response to the gastrin, and which has a gastrin-secreting tumor?
blocks.explain: Both can have ECL hyperplasia, because gastrin is trophic whatever its source. The patient with pH 7 has achlorhydria and appropriate gastrin release from intact antral G cells. The patient with pH 1.5 has inappropriate gastrin with acid hypersecretion, which points to a gastrinoma.

sections.title: Celiac disease: mucosal lesion and its consequences

blocks.text: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten proteins in wheat, barley, and rye in people who carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Gliadin peptides are rich in proline and glutamine, which makes them resistant to gastric, pancreatic, and brush border proteases, so long fragments reach the lamina propria.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of celiac disease
steps: Protease-resistant gliadin peptides cross the epithelium
Tissue transglutaminase deamidates glutamine to glutamate
Negatively charged peptides bind HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 tightly
Gluten-specific CD4 T cells release interferon gamma
IL-15 activates CD8 intraepithelial lymphocytes to kill enterocytes
Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia
blocks.caption: Deamidation by tissue transglutaminase is the step that makes gluten strongly immunogenic in genetically susceptible people.

blocks.text: B cells that recognize tissue transglutaminase complexed with gliadin receive help from gluten-specific T cells, which explains why the disease produces IgA antibodies against a self enzyme. IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and IgA antiendomysial antibodies (endomysial antigen is tissue transglutaminase) fall when gluten is removed. Selective IgA deficiency is more common in celiac disease and makes IgA tests falsely negative, so total IgA is measured.

The biopsy shows three linked changes. Intraepithelial lymphocytes increase first and are the most sensitive finding. Enterocytes are killed faster than they are replaced, so villi shorten and flatten (villous atrophy), and the crypts lengthen and show more mitoses (crypt hyperplasia) as they try to restore the epithelium. The lamina propria fills with plasma cells and lymphocytes. Injury is greatest in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, where gluten arrives at the highest concentration, and lessens distally.

That distribution explains the deficiencies. Iron, folate, and calcium are absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, so iron deficiency anemia that does not respond to oral iron is a common presentation, often without diarrhea. Folate deficiency can make the anemia mixed, and calcium and vitamin D malabsorption cause osteopenia. B12, absorbed in the terminal ileum, is usually spared. Lost surface area causes diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, bloating, and failure to thrive in children, and loss of tip enzymes causes secondary lactase deficiency. D-xylose absorption is low.

blocks.title: Extraintestinal findings of celiac disease
rows: IgA against epidermal transglutaminase deposits granularly in dermal papillae; neutrophil microabscesses and subepidermal vesicles that itch intensely on elbows, knees, and buttocks
Chronically stimulated intraepithelial T cells undergo clonal expansion; suspect it when symptoms return despite strict gluten avoidance
Shared HLA risk: type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis
blocks.caption: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin expression of gluten sensitivity and shares the transglutaminase-directed IgA response of the gut disease.

sections.title: Pancreatic enzyme deficiency versus mucosal disease

blocks.text: Absorption needs three phases in sequence. In the luminal phase, pancreatic enzymes and bile acids break down and solubilize nutrients. In the mucosal phase, brush border enzymes finish digestion and enterocytes take up the products. In the postabsorptive phase, chylomicrons and other products leave through lymph and blood. Malabsorption is classified by the phase that fails, and two tests separate the first two phases.

Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, ductal obstruction by tumor, or pancreatic resection) is a luminal phase failure. Lipase has almost no backup, so fat malabsorption appears once lipase output falls to roughly 10% of normal, producing bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools, weight loss, and deficiencies of vitamins A, D, E, and K. Protein malabsorption (azotorrhea) accompanies it. Carbohydrate digestion is better preserved because salivary amylase and brush border enzymes take over. Pancreatic proteases normally free B12 from haptocorrin, so B12 absorption can also be impaired.

Fecal elastase tests the pancreas: it is secreted by acinar cells and is not degraded in transit, so a low stool level means low pancreatic output. D-xylose tests the mucosa: it is a pentose that needs no digestion and is absorbed in the proximal small bowel, so after an oral dose its blood and urine levels reflect mucosal uptake. It is normal in pancreatic insufficiency and low in mucosal disease such as celiac disease. A low result can also come from bacterial overgrowth (bacteria consume xylose), slow gastric emptying, or reduced renal excretion.

blocks.title: Separating luminal from mucosal malabsorption
rows: Low, corrects after bacteria are cleared
blocks.caption: Steatorrhea shows that fat is lost; fecal elastase and D-xylose show where the process failed.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading steatorrhea
blocks.text: A man with years of heavy alcohol use has weight loss and greasy stools. Fecal fat is 25 g per day (steatorrhea is above about 7 g). Fecal elastase is low and D-xylose absorption is normal. Step 1: fat is malabsorbed. Step 2: normal D-xylose means enterocytes absorb a sugar that needs no digestion, so the mucosa works. Step 3: low elastase means acinar output is reduced. The failure is luminal, from chronic pancreatitis. If instead D-xylose were low and elastase normal, the mucosa would be at fault, and a duodenal biopsy would look for celiac disease.

Enteropeptidase shows why one brush border enzyme can control all pancreatic proteolysis. Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens so they cannot digest the gland. Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cleaves the activation peptide from trypsinogen, and trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and the other zymogens: chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, the procarboxypeptidases, prophospholipase A2, and procolipase. Without enteropeptidase the cascade never starts, even though the pancreas secretes normal amounts of zymogen.

Congenital enteropeptidase deficiency, a rare autosomal recessive disorder, presents in infancy with diarrhea, failure to thrive, and hypoproteinemia with edema from protein malabsorption. The pancreas and the mucosa are structurally normal, and D-xylose absorption is normal.

Lactase (lactase-phlorizin hydrolase) is a brush border enzyme that splits lactose into glucose and galactose, which enterocytes then absorb through SGLT1. It is most active in the jejunum, is expressed most strongly on mature enterocytes toward the villus tips, and has the lowest activity of the disaccharidases, so it is the first to become rate limiting when it falls.

Primary (adult-type) lactase deficiency, also called lactase nonpersistence, is a genetically programmed fall in lactase expression after weaning. It is the usual state of most adults worldwide and is especially common in people of East Asian, West African, and Native American ancestry, while lactase persistence is common in people of northern European ancestry. The villi and the other disaccharidases are normal, so the biopsy is normal and D-xylose absorption is normal. Secondary lactase deficiency follows injury to the villus tips, as after viral enteritis such as rotavirus, giardiasis, or celiac disease, and recovers as the mucosa heals. Congenital lactase deficiency, present from birth, is rare.

blocks.title: From undigested lactose to symptoms
steps: Lactose reaches the distal bowel undigested
Unabsorbed sugar holds water in the lumen
Colonic bacteria ferment lactose
Short-chain fatty acids acidify the stool
Hydrogen, methane, and carbon dioxide distend the colon
Hydrogen is absorbed into blood and exhaled
blocks.caption: Osmotic water retention causes diarrhea; fermentation causes gas, bloating, cramps, flatulence, and the breath test signal.

blocks.text: Unabsorbed lactose is osmotically active, so water stays in the lumen and stool volume rises. Colonic fermentation salvages part of the sugar as short-chain fatty acids, but the gas and acid cause bloating, cramping, and flatulence within about 30 minutes to a few hours of eating dairy. Symptoms depend on dose: many people with nonpersistence tolerate small amounts of lactose.

The stool chemistry shows the mechanism. The stool osmotic gap, calculated as 290 minus 2 times the sum of stool Na+ and K+ (in mOsm/kg), is large in osmotic diarrhea (commonly above about 100 to 125) because an unmeasured solute holds water. In secretory diarrhea it is small (below about 50) because electrolytes account for the osmolality. Stool pH is low, often below about 6, from fermentation acids. Because the cause is a substance the patient eats, diarrhea stops with fasting, whereas secretory diarrhea continues.

The hydrogen breath test measures exhaled hydrogen after a lactose load; human cells make no hydrogen, so a rise of about 20 parts per million or more over baseline means bacteria fermented lactose that the small bowel failed to absorb. False negatives occur when the colonic flora produces methane instead of hydrogen or has been suppressed. Lactase deficiency does not cause steatorrhea, weight loss, or vitamin deficiency on its own; those findings point to an underlying mucosal disease with secondary lactase loss.

blocks.predict: A patient with chronic watery diarrhea is admitted and given nothing by mouth for 48 hours. The diarrhea stops. Stool Na+ was 30 and K+ was 40 mmol/L before fasting. Is this osmotic or secretory diarrhea?
blocks.explain: Osmotic. The gap is 290 minus 2 times 70, which is 150 mOsm/kg, showing an unmeasured solute. Diarrhea that stops when intake stops is driven by something ingested, such as lactose. Secretory diarrhea from toxins or hormones has a small gap and continues during fasting.
blocks.check: The stool osmotic gap and fasting paragraph.

sections.title: Short bowel syndrome and the consequences of ileal resection

blocks.text: Short bowel syndrome is malabsorption caused by loss of functional small intestinal length, usually after extensive resection for Crohn disease, mesenteric ischemia, volvulus, or trauma in adults and necrotizing enterocolitis or congenital anomalies in children. It is commonly defined as less than about 200 cm of remaining small bowel. Its consequences depend on how much bowel remains, which segment was removed, and whether the colon is still in continuity.

blocks.title: What each segment contributes
rows: Most digestion and nutrient absorption; leaky epithelium, limited water salvage
Ileum can adapt and take over nutrient absorption
B12 and intrinsic factor uptake by cubilin; Na+-dependent bile acid uptake; tight epithelium salvages Na+ and water; L cells release PYY and GLP-1 to slow transit
B12 deficiency, bile acid loss, faster transit; no other segment replaces these functions
Slows transit; limits reflux of colonic bacteria
Absorbs water and Na+; ferments unabsorbed carbohydrate to short-chain fatty acids
blocks.caption: Losing the ileum has worse long-term consequences than losing an equal length of jejunum.

blocks.text: Diarrhea has several causes: less surface area, faster transit, unabsorbed solute, and, after massive resection, transient gastric acid hypersecretion that inactivates pancreatic lipase in the duodenum. Steatorrhea causes deficiencies of vitamins A, D, E, and K and binds calcium and magnesium in the lumen.

Ileal resection breaks the enterohepatic circulation, which normally returns about 95% of secreted bile acids. After a short resection (commonly quoted as under about 100 cm), the liver increases synthesis enough to maintain micelles, but bile acids spilling into the colon stimulate Cl- and water secretion, causing watery bile acid diarrhea with little steatorrhea. After a longer resection, losses exceed hepatic synthesis, the bile acid pool shrinks, micelles fail, and steatorrhea dominates. Removing more than about 60 cm of terminal ileum usually causes B12 deficiency, which appears only after years because the liver stores several years of B12. A depleted bile acid pool also makes bile supersaturated with cholesterol and raises the risk of gallstones.

blocks.title: Worked example: short versus long ileal resection
blocks.text: Patient A had 50 cm of terminal ileum removed; patient B had 150 cm. Both have diarrhea. In patient A, the liver replaces lost bile acids, micelles form, and fat is absorbed, but the bile acids that reach the colon cause secretory diarrhea, so fecal fat is near normal. In patient B, synthesis cannot keep pace, micelles fail, and fecal fat is high; unabsorbed long-chain fatty acids reaching the colon add to the diarrhea. B12 deficiency is expected in patient B and may occur in patient A, since the cutoff of about 60 cm is approximate.

Enteric hyperoxaluria explains the kidney stones. Normally dietary oxalate binds calcium in the lumen to form insoluble calcium oxalate, which is excreted in stool. When fat is malabsorbed, fatty acids bind calcium as soaps, leaving oxalate soluble, and bile acids and fatty acids also make the colonic mucosa more permeable to it. The colon absorbs the free oxalate, the kidney excretes it, and calcium oxalate stones form, made more likely by low urine volume, citrate, and magnesium from diarrhea. Patients with an end jejunostomy and no colon do not develop enteric hyperoxaluria.

blocks.title: Ileal resection to calcium oxalate stones
steps: Terminal ileum lost; bile acids not reabsorbed
Bile acid pool shrinks and fat is malabsorbed
Luminal fatty acids bind calcium as soaps
Dietary oxalate stays free and soluble
Colon absorbs the free oxalate
Urinary oxalate rises; calcium oxalate stones form
blocks.caption: The colon must be present, because it is the site of excess oxalate absorption.

blocks.text: Over months to about two years the remaining bowel adapts: villi lengthen, crypts deepen, and the lumen dilates, driven by luminal nutrients and trophic hormones such as GLP-2. Adaptation is greatest in the ileum, which is another reason that preserving ileum matters.

sections.title: Blind loop syndrome and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

blocks.text: The proximal small bowel normally holds relatively few bacteria, commonly quoted as fewer than about 10 to the 3rd to 10 to the 4th organisms per mL, compared with about 10 to the 11th or more per gram in the colon. Gastric acid, the migrating motor complex that sweeps the lumen between meals, the ileocecal valve, secretory IgA, and bile keep it that way. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) follows when stasis or loss of these defenses lets colonic-type flora, including anaerobes such as Bacteroides and Clostridium species, multiply proximally.

A blind loop is a segment that food bypasses, so it does not empty. Classic examples after gastric surgery are the afferent (duodenal) limb of a Billroth II gastrojejunostomy and other surgically created loops. Strictures, jejunal diverticula, fistulas, motility disorders such as scleroderma and diabetic neuropathy, resection of the ileocecal valve, and achlorhydria cause the same overgrowth.

blocks.title: How bacterial overgrowth causes malabsorption
steps: Stasis lets anaerobes multiply in the small bowel
Bacterial hydrolases deconjugate bile acids
Free bile acids are absorbed early and fail to form micelles
Fat and fat-soluble vitamins are malabsorbed (steatorrhea)
Bacteria take up B12 before it reaches the ileum
Bacteria synthesize folate, which the host absorbs
blocks.caption: Two vitamins move in opposite directions: B12 falls while folate stays normal or rises.

blocks.text: Conjugation with glycine or taurine lowers the pKa of bile acids, so they stay ionized, cannot cross the jejunal membrane, and remain in the lumen to form micelles until the ileal transporter reclaims them. Bacterial bile salt hydrolases remove the glycine or taurine. The unconjugated bile acids are absorbed passively in the jejunum, so their luminal concentration falls below that needed for micelles, and fat digestion products are not solubilized. Free bile acids also injure enterocytes, causing patchy villus damage and loss of brush border enzymes such as lactase.

Anaerobes take up B12, including B12 bound to intrinsic factor, so less reaches the ileal receptor and a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia can develop. Intrinsic factor secretion and the ileum are normal, which separates this from pernicious anemia and ileal resection. Because the bacteria synthesize folate, serum folate is normal or raised, a key clue. Bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate produces gas, bloating, and an early rise in breath hydrogen after a glucose or lactulose load, and bacteria also consume D-xylose, so its absorption is low but corrects when the bacteria are cleared.

blocks.title: Sorting causes of B12 deficiency
blocks.caption: The last column follows the logic of the classic Schilling test, now rarely available, which boards may still use to frame these distinctions.

blocks.predict: A patient with a Billroth II gastrojejunostomy has steatorrhea, macrocytic anemia, low serum B12, and a high serum folate. Why does folate rise while B12 falls?
blocks.explain: Anaerobes in the stagnant afferent loop take up B12 before it reaches the ileum but synthesize folate, which the jejunum absorbs. Deconjugated bile acids are absorbed too early to form micelles, causing the steatorrhea.
blocks.check: The flow and the B12 paragraph in this section.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology organize this chapter. Acid comes from the gastric body, iron and folate are absorbed proximally, and B12 and bile acids are reclaimed in the terminal ileum, so the location of disease predicts the deficiency: microcytic anemia points to the stomach or duodenum, macrocytic anemia with low B12 points to the stomach, the ileum, or bacteria, and folate separates bacteria (high) from the others. Biochemistry explains why a single step can fail completely, as with enteropeptidase starting the zymogen cascade or bile acid conjugation setting where bile acids are absorbed.

Immunology and pathology explain chronic risk. Autoimmune gastritis and celiac disease are T cell diseases with antibodies used as markers, and both carry neoplastic risk from chronic stimulation: gastrin-driven carcinoid in the stomach and T cell lymphoma in the small bowel. Microbiology enters through the acid barrier and stasis, and renal pathology through oxalate. The tests have limits: D-xylose depends on gastric emptying and renal function, IgA serology fails in IgA deficiency, and breath tests miss methane producers, so each result is read with the whole picture.

summary: Achlorhydria removes the acid-somatostatin brake on G cells; with the antrum spared, gastrin rises and drives ECL hyperplasia and type 1 carcinoid.
Loss of acid impairs iron solubility and release of food-bound B12; autoimmune gastritis adds intrinsic factor loss and pernicious anemia.

In celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin so it binds HLA-DQ2 or DQ8, causing intraepithelial lymphocytosis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia worst in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum.
Celiac disease presents with iron deficiency refractory to oral iron, dermatitis herpetiformis (IgA in dermal papillae), and risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.
Steatorrhea with low fecal elastase and normal D-xylose means pancreatic insufficiency; low D-xylose means mucosal disease or bacterial overgrowth.
Enteropeptidase starts the zymogen cascade, so its deficiency blocks all protease activation and causes infant protein malabsorption with edema.
Lactase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhea with a large stool osmotic gap, acidic stool, a positive hydrogen breath test, and relief with fasting; villi are normal in the primary form.
Terminal ileal loss causes B12 deficiency and bile acid loss: bile acid diarrhea after short resections, steatorrhea after long ones.
Fat malabsorption with an intact colon frees oxalate from calcium, causing enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones.
Blind loop overgrowth deconjugates bile acids (steatorrhea) and consumes B12 while making folate, giving low B12 with normal or high folate.

verify: Threshold values vary between sources: steatorrhea above about 7 g of fat per day, fecal elastase below about 200 micrograms per gram as abnormal, a breath hydrogen rise of about 20 ppm, osmotic gap cutoffs of about 100 to 125 and 50 mOsm/kg, and stool pH below about 6. Confirm the values NABNE expects.

Short bowel syndrome is defined in different sources as less than about 200 cm of remaining small bowel; the 100 cm cutoff between bile acid diarrhea and steatorrhea and the 60 cm cutoff for B12 deficiency are approximate teaching values.
The SIBO threshold on jejunal aspirate is quoted as at least 10 to the 3rd or at least 10 to the 5th organisms per mL depending on the source.
The statement that steatorrhea appears when lipase output falls to about 10% of normal is a classic teaching value; confirm wording.

Celiac lesion distribution is given here as worst in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum as in the competency; current biopsy practice samples the duodenal bulb and distal duodenum. Confirm the phrasing NABNE uses.
The Schilling test is mentioned only as historical reasoning; confirm whether NABNE still frames B12 questions with it.
Fecal elastase is shown as normal in celiac disease; it can be modestly low with severe villous atrophy (reduced CCK release), so confirm the expected answer.
Requested new diagram name for a future revision: absorption-sites (stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon with iron, folate, B12, bile acids, and oxalate sites).
